510: 
511: % ======================================================================
512: \section{Appendix: usage examples}
513: \label{app:examples}
514: % ======================================================================
515: 
516: Command-line recipes for the most frequent use cases, checked against version V66. Commands use \code{compass.py} as the executable name, a copy of the current simulator version (\code{compass\_simV66.py}) kept under this stable name for daily use, so the examples can be copied and pasted directly. A final backslash indicates shell line continuation.
517: 
518: \subsection*{B.1 --- Basic execution (dipolar equilibrium)}
519: 
520: Square $8\times8$ array with all defaults (steel needle with automatically computed moment and inertia, no external field):
521: \begin{verbatim}
522: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --geometry square
523: \end{verbatim}
524: Generates summary images (initial state, equilibrium, comparison, order parameter) and \code{compass\_field\_log.csv} in the current directory. For the other lattices: \code{--geometry triangular} or \code{--geometry honeycomb}.
525: 
526: \subsection*{B.2 --- GPU on and off}
527: 
528: CPU is the default (\code{--gpu 0}). With V40 optimization, the CPU already handles medium arrays in seconds; GPU is useful for large arrays:
529: \begin{verbatim}
530: # CPU (default) -- medium array
531: python3 compass.py --N 30 --M 30 --t_sim 5.0
532: 
533: # GPU (CuPy/RTX 3090) -- large array; requires cupy installed
534: python3 compass.py --N 60 --M 60 --t_sim 5.0 --gpu 1
535: \end{verbatim}
536: With \code{--gpu 1}, video encoding also uses the NVENC hardware encoder when available. If CuPy is not functional, the program warns and automatically falls back to CPU.
537: 
538: \subsection*{B.3 --- Video and figures in good resolution}
539: 
540: For arrays above $15\times15$, use \code{--dpi} 150--200. Smaller \code{--frame\_every} = smoother animation (more frames):
541: \begin{verbatim}
542: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --t_sim 4.0 \
543:     --video demo --dpi 180 --fps 30 --frame_every 3
544: \end{verbatim}
545: The video receives automatic numbering (\code{demo0000.mp4}, \code{demo0001.mp4}, \dots). To keep individual frame PNGs after assembling the video, add \code{--keep\_frames}. For static high-resolution figures only (no video), omit \code{--video} and use \code{--dpi 200}.
546: 
547: \subsection*{B.4 --- Fast sweeps: no images, no bar}
548: 
549: In campaigns with many executions, turn off all image generation (data CSVs are kept) and the progress bar:
550: \begin{verbatim}
551: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --t_sim 1.0 \
552:     --make_images 0 --progress_bar 0
553: \end{verbatim}
554: Speedup of $\sim 3\times$ in small arrays, where rendering dominates time. For \emph{uniform}-length time series across runs (no early stops by $S{=}1.00$, rest, or equilibrium), add \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} (V42).
555: 
556: \subsection*{B.5 --- Damping control (dynamic regimes)}
557: 
558: The regime is characterized by the quality factor $Q$, printed in the header of each run along with the classification (under-/overdamped). The exact $Q$ depends on the dominant field (dipolar or external); the values below, with all other parameters at default, illustrate the three regimes:
559: \begin{verbatim}
560: # underdamped (Q >> 1): visibly oscillates before stabilizing
561: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-8 --video sub
562: 
563: # intermediate (Q ~ 1): crossover
564: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 1e-6 --video middle
565: 
566: # overdamped (Q << 1): monotonic relaxation, no oscillation
567: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-5 --video over
568: \end{verbatim}
569: Check the printed $Q$ in the header and adjust \code{--damping} until the desired regime is reached. \code{--damping 0} disables dissipation (perpetual oscillation).
570: 
571: \subsection*{B.6 --- Needle size and spacing}
572: 
573: The radius $R$ of the circumscribed circle defines lattice spacing ($r_{nn} = 2R$); \code{--needle\_frac} defines needle length as a fraction of $2R$; sheet thickness affects automatic inertia and moment calculations:
574: \begin{verbatim}
575: # needles with 1 cm radius, occupying half the available diameter
576: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --R 0.01 --needle_frac 0.5
577: 
578: # thinner sheet (0.2 mm): lighter needle -> oscillates faster
579: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --needle_thickness 2e-4
580: 
581: # override automatic calculations with explicit values
582: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --moment 0.05 --inertia 1e-9
583: \end{verbatim}
584: 
585: \subsection*{B.7 --- External field: the six modes}
586: 
587: One example per mode, covering the full range of \code{--field\_mode}. The amplitude is \code{--B\_ext} and the direction is \code{--phi\_ext}.
588: 
589: \medskip\noindent\textbf{(1) static} --- constant (or zero) field throughout the simulation:
590: \begin{verbatim}
591: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --B_ext 1e-3 --phi_ext 45
592: \end{verbatim}
593: 
594: \noindent\textbf{(2) hysteresis} --- five-ramp cycle ($0 \to +B_{\max} \to 0 \to -B_{\max} \to 0 \to +B_{\max}$). The video (V45) shows needles and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time, side by side. Spacing can be \code{linear} (default) or \code{log} ($\sim$15$\times$ finer sampling in the coercivity region):
595: \begin{verbatim}
596: # linear, with dual-panel video (needles + M x H curve)
597: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
598:     --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0 --video hist --dpi 160
599: 
600: # log-symmetric spacing (fine near B=0)
601: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
602:     --hyst_spacing log --hyst_log_k 5 --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0
603: \end{verbatim}
604: 
605: \noindent\textbf{(3) sine} --- sinusoidal field $B(t) = B_{\max}\sin(2\pi f t)$; \code{--t\_sim} should cover several periods:
606: \begin{verbatim}
607: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode sine \
608:     --B_ext 0.002 --field_freq 0.5 --t_sim 8.0
609: \end{verbatim}
610: 
611: \noindent\textbf{(4) pulse} --- wait \code{field\_delay}, apply for \code{t\_pulse}, set to zero, and stabilize (equilibrium by $\omega$ and torque). If \code{--t\_pulse} is omitted, the legacy criterion is used (field until $S \geq 0.99$ or plateau):
612: \begin{verbatim}
613: # timed: wait 0.2 s -> field 0.3 s -> zero and stabilize
614: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
615:     --field_delay 0.2 --t_pulse 0.3 --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0
616: 
617: # legacy (without t_pulse): field until saturation, then relaxation
618: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
619:     --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0
620: \end{verbatim}
621: 
622: \noindent\textbf{(5) step\_pos} --- $B{=}0$ for \code{field\_delay}, then field switched on and held until the end:
623: \begin{verbatim}
624: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_pos \
625:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
626: \end{verbatim}
627: 
628: \noindent\textbf{(6) step\_neg} --- field from $t{=}0$, removed at \code{field\_delay}, then kept at zero until the end:
629: \begin{verbatim}
630: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_neg \
631:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
632: \end{verbatim}
633: 
634: \noindent In \code{hysteresis}, the $M(B)$ loop is exported to \code{hysteresis\_loop.csv}; in \code{sine}, to \code{sine\_field.csv}. In pulse/step modes, \code{--torque\_tol} controls the equilibrium criterion and \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} disables early stopping (Appendix~A).
635: 
636: \subsection*{B.8 --- Magnetic-domain visualization}
637: 
638: Demonstration scenario producing clear, well-separated domains (square lattice with low initial noise and long relaxation):
639: \begin{verbatim}
640: python3 compass.py --N 24 --M 24 --R 0.01 --noise 0.6 \
641:     --t_sim 8.0 --damping 3e-6 \
642:     --halo_mode domains --domain_tol 35 --video domains --dpi 160
643: \end{verbatim}
644: Each connected region of needles with similar orientation (within \code{--domain\_tol} degrees) receives a color; small domains appear in gray. Smaller tolerances, for example the default $15^\circ$, fragment more; larger tolerances aggregate more. From V43 onward, halos (domain or order) appear in \emph{all} figures: \code{compass\_initial}, \code{compass\_equilibrium}, video frames, and also \code{compass\_comparison}, whose panels show the domain count for each state in the title.
645: 
646: \subsection*{B.9 --- Periodic boundary conditions and reproducibility}
647: 
648: \begin{verbatim}
649: # array treated as an infinite periodic structure (1 replica per side)
650: python3 compass.py --N 16 --M 16 --pbc 1 --pbc_images 1
651: 
652: # exact reproducibility: fix the initial-noise seed
653: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --seed 123
654: \end{verbatim}
655: 
656: \subsection*{B.10 --- Full scientific campaign (satellite scripts)}
657: 
658: The simulation campaign sweep scripts are designed to run programmatic sweeps over multiple values of damping (friction), initial seeds (noise realizations), and lattice geometries to generate statistical datasets for hysteresis loop shape and avalanche scaling analysis. 
659: 
660: These scripts import from the core simulation file (\code{compass.py}) and call the simulator API (\code{relax()}) directly.
661: 
662: \subsubsection*{1. Serial Campaign Execution (\code{damping\_sweep.py})}
663: The \code{damping\_sweep.py} script executes a serial sweep across geometries, seeds, and damping coefficients. It performs Stage 1 (hysteresis) followed by Stage 2 (field-free relaxation for domain statistics).
664: 
665: \begin{verbatim}
666: # Quick test to validate the pipeline (low resolution, short runtime):
667: python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir results_quick --quick_test 1
668: 
669: # Full campaign (sequential sweep, may take several hours on CPU):
670: python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir results_campaign \

A manifest (\code{manifest.csv}) tracks the completion status of each run, enabling resumption if the campaign is interrupted.

511: % ======================================================================
512: \section{Appendix: usage examples}
513: \label{app:examples}
514: % ======================================================================
515: 
516: Command-line recipes for the most frequent use cases, checked against version V66. Commands use \code{compass.py} as the executable name, a copy of the current simulator version (\code{compass\_simV66.py}) kept under this stable name for daily use, so the examples can be copied and pasted directly. A final backslash indicates shell line continuation.
517: 
518: \subsection*{B.1 --- Basic execution (dipolar equilibrium)}
519: 
520: Square $8\times8$ array with all defaults (steel needle with automatically computed moment and inertia, no external field):
521: \begin{verbatim}
522: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --geometry square
523: \end{verbatim}
524: Generates summary images (initial state, equilibrium, comparison, order parameter) and \code{compass\_field\_log.csv} in the current directory. For the other lattices: \code{--geometry triangular} or \code{--geometry honeycomb}.
525: 
526: \subsection*{B.2 --- GPU on and off}
527: 
528: CPU is the default (\code{--gpu 0}). With V40 optimization, the CPU already handles medium arrays in seconds; GPU is useful for large arrays:
529: \begin{verbatim}
530: # CPU (default) -- medium array
531: python3 compass.py --N 30 --M 30 --t_sim 5.0
532: 
533: # GPU (CuPy/RTX 3090) -- large array; requires cupy installed
534: python3 compass.py --N 60 --M 60 --t_sim 5.0 --gpu 1
535: \end{verbatim}
536: With \code{--gpu 1}, video encoding also uses the NVENC hardware encoder when available. If CuPy is not functional, the program warns and automatically falls back to CPU.
537: 
538: \subsection*{B.3 --- Video and figures in good resolution}
539: 
540: For arrays above $15\times15$, use \code{--dpi} 150--200. Smaller \code{--frame\_every} = smoother animation (more frames):
541: \begin{verbatim}
542: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --t_sim 4.0 \
543:     --video demo --dpi 180 --fps 30 --frame_every 3
544: \end{verbatim}
545: The video receives automatic numbering (\code{demo0000.mp4}, \code{demo0001.mp4}, \dots). To keep individual frame PNGs after assembling the video, add \code{--keep\_frames}. For static high-resolution figures only (no video), omit \code{--video} and use \code{--dpi 200}.
546: 
547: \subsection*{B.4 --- Fast sweeps: no images, no bar}
548: 
549: In campaigns with many executions, turn off all image generation (data CSVs are kept) and the progress bar:
550: \begin{verbatim}
551: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --t_sim 1.0 \
552:     --make_images 0 --progress_bar 0
553: \end{verbatim}
554: Speedup of $\sim 3\times$ in small arrays, where rendering dominates time. For \emph{uniform}-length time series across runs (no early stops by $S{=}1.00$, rest, or equilibrium), add \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} (V42).
555: 
556: \subsection*{B.5 --- Damping control (dynamic regimes)}
557: 
558: The regime is characterized by the quality factor $Q$, printed in the header of each run along with the classification (under-/overdamped). The exact $Q$ depends on the dominant field (dipolar or external); the values below, with all other parameters at default, illustrate the three regimes:
559: \begin{verbatim}
560: # underdamped (Q >> 1): visibly oscillates before stabilizing
561: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-8 --video sub
562: 
563: # intermediate (Q ~ 1): crossover
564: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 1e-6 --video middle
565: 
566: # overdamped (Q << 1): monotonic relaxation, no oscillation
567: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-5 --video over
568: \end{verbatim}
569: Check the printed $Q$ in the header and adjust \code{--damping} until the desired regime is reached. \code{--damping 0} disables dissipation (perpetual oscillation).
570: 
571: \subsection*{B.6 --- Needle size and spacing}
572: 
573: The radius $R$ of the circumscribed circle defines lattice spacing ($r_{nn} = 2R$); \code{--needle\_frac} defines needle length as a fraction of $2R$; sheet thickness affects automatic inertia and moment calculations:
574: \begin{verbatim}
575: # needles with 1 cm radius, occupying half the available diameter
576: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --R 0.01 --needle_frac 0.5
577: 
578: # thinner sheet (0.2 mm): lighter needle -> oscillates faster
579: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --needle_thickness 2e-4
580: 
581: # override automatic calculations with explicit values
582: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --moment 0.05 --inertia 1e-9
583: \end{verbatim}
584: 
585: \subsection*{B.7 --- External field: the six modes}
586: 
587: One example per mode, covering the full range of \code{--field\_mode}. The amplitude is \code{--B\_ext} and the direction is \code{--phi\_ext}.
588: 
589: \medskip\noindent\textbf{(1) static} --- constant (or zero) field throughout the simulation:
590: \begin{verbatim}
591: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --B_ext 1e-3 --phi_ext 45
592: \end{verbatim}
593: 
594: \noindent\textbf{(2) hysteresis} --- five-ramp cycle ($0 \to +B_{\max} \to 0 \to -B_{\max} \to 0 \to +B_{\max}$). The video (V45) shows needles and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time, side by side. Spacing can be \code{linear} (default) or \code{log} ($\sim$15$\times$ finer sampling in the coercivity region):
595: \begin{verbatim}
596: # linear, with dual-panel video (needles + M x H curve)
597: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
598:     --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0 --video hist --dpi 160
599:

\subsection*{B.5 --- Damping control (dynamic regimes)}

The regime is characterized by the quality factor $Q$, printed in the header of each run along with the classification (under-/overdamped). The exact $Q$ depends on the dominant field (dipolar or external); the values below, with all other parameters at default, illustrate the three regimes. Additionally, per-needle random damping noise can be modeled with \code{--damping\_noise}:
\begin{verbatim}
# underdamped (Q >> 1): visibly oscillates before stabilizing
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-8 --video sub

# intermediate (Q ~ 1): crossover
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 1e-6 --video middle

# overdamped (Q << 1): monotonic relaxation, no oscillation
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-5 --video over

# underdamped with random per-needle damping noise (up to 20% variation)
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-8 --damping_noise 0.2
\end{verbatim}
Check the printed $Q$ in the header and adjust \code{--damping} until the desired regime is reached. \code{--damping 0} disables dissipation (perpetual oscillation).

\subsection*{B.6 --- Needle size and spacing}

The radius $R$ of the circumscribed circle defines lattice spacing ($r_{nn} = 2R$); \code{--needle\_frac} defines needle length as a fraction of $2R$; sheet thickness affects automatic inertia and moment calculations. You can also customize steel density and saturation induction, or override calculations with explicit moment and inertia values:
\begin{verbatim}
# needles with 1 cm radius, occupying half the available diameter
python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --R 0.01 --needle_frac 0.5

# thinner sheet (0.2 mm): lighter needle -> oscillates faster
python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --needle_thickness 2e-4

# custom steel material parameters (density and saturation)
python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --steel_density 7800 --steel_Bsat 1.8

# override automatic calculations with explicit values
python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --moment 0.05 --inertia 1e-9
\end{verbatim}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{(1) static} --- constant (or zero) field throughout the simulation. It can be defined in polar coordinates or using independent Cartesian components:
\begin{verbatim}
# defined by field intensity and angle (45 degrees)
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --B_ext 1e-3 --phi_ext 45

# equivalent field using Cartesian components (Bx = By = 0.707 mT)
python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --ext_Bx 0.000707 --ext_By 0.000707
\end{verbatim}

\noindent\textbf{(2) hysteresis} --- five-ramp cycle ($0 \to +B_{\max} \to 0 \to -B_{\max} \to 0 \to +B_{\max}$). The video (V45) shows needles and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time, side by side. Spacing can be \code{linear} (default) or \code{log} ($\sim$15$\times$ finer sampling in the coercivity region). Automatic axis scaling for the curve can be enabled via \code{--hyst\_autoscale}:
\begin{verbatim}
# linear, with dual-panel video (needles + M x H curve)
python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
    --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0 --video hist --dpi 160

# log-symmetric spacing (fine near B=0) with autoscaled M x H axes
python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
    --hyst_spacing log --hyst_log_k 5 --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0 \
    --hyst_autoscale 1
\end{verbatim}

621: \noindent\textbf{(3) sine} --- sinusoidal field $B(t) = B_{\max}\sin(2\pi f t)$; \code{--t\_sim} should cover several periods:
622: \begin{verbatim}
623: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode sine \
624:     --B_ext 0.002 --field_freq 0.5 --t_sim 8.0
625: \end{verbatim}
626: 
627: \noindent\textbf{(4) pulse} --- wait \code{field\_delay}, apply for \code{t\_pulse}, set to zero, and stabilize (equilibrium by $\omega$ and torque). If \code{--t\_pulse} is omitted, the legacy criterion is used (field until $S \geq 0.99$ or plateau). The torque tolerance for early termination can be adjusted via \code{--torque\_tol}:
628: \begin{verbatim}
629: # timed: wait 0.2 s -> field 0.3 s -> zero and stabilize (tighter torque tolerance)
630: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
631:     --field_delay 0.2 --t_pulse 0.3 --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0 \
632:     --torque_tol 1e-4
633: 
634: # legacy (without t_pulse): field until saturation, then relaxation
635: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
636:     --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0
637: \end{verbatim}
638: 
639: \noindent\textbf{(5) step\_pos} --- $B{=}0$ for \code{field\_delay}, then field switched on and held until the end:
640: \begin{verbatim}
641: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_pos \
642:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
643: \end{verbatim}
644: 
645: \noindent\textbf{(6) step\_neg} --- field from $t{=}0$, removed at \code{field\_delay}, then kept at zero until the end:
646: \begin{verbatim}
647: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_neg \
648:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
649: \end{verbatim}
650: 
651: \noindent In \code{hysteresis}, the $M(B)$ loop is exported to \code{hysteresis\_loop.csv}; in \code{sine}, to \code{sine\_field.csv}. In pulse/step modes, \code{--torque\_tol} controls the equilibrium criterion and \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} disables early stopping (Appendix~A).
652: 
653: \subsection*{B.8 --- Magnetic-domain visualization}
654: 
655: Demonstration scenario producing clear, well-separated domains (square lattice with low initial noise and long relaxation):
656: \begin{verbatim}
657: python3 compass.py --N 24 --M 24 --R 0.01 --noise 0.6 \
658:     --t_sim 8.0 --damping 3e-6 \
659:     --halo_mode domains --domain_tol 35 --video domains --dpi 160
660: \end{verbatim}
661: Each connected region of needles with similar orientation (within \code{--domain\_tol} degrees) receives a color; small domains appear in gray. Smaller tolerances, for example the default $15^\circ$, fragment more; larger tolerances aggregate more. From V43 onward, halos (domain or order) appear in \emph{all} figures: \code{compass\_initial}, \code{compass\_equilibrium}, video frames, and also \code{compass\_comparison}, whose panels show the domain count for each state in the title.
662:

666: # array treated as an infinite periodic structure (1 replica per side)
667: python3 compass.py --N 16 --M 16 --pbc 1 --pbc_images 1
668: 
669: # exact reproducibility (fixed seed) with a custom (tighter) integration step factor
670: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --seed 123 --dt_factor 0.01

damping_sweep.py
=================

Simulation campaign for the central study:
    "How does the damping coefficient control the shape of the
    hysteresis loop and the statistics of avalanches in classical dipolar
    lattices, and how does this depend on the geometry (square / triangular /
    honeycomb)?"

This script DOES NOT modify compass.py. It imports the module and calls
relax() programmatically, sweeping:

    damping  x  seed  x  geometry

for the field mode 'hysteresis' (Stage 1) and 'static' B=0 (Stage 2,
free relaxation for domain statistics).

Output
------
For each run, saves a CSV with the complete field_log:
    out_dir/hysteresis/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.csv
    out_dir/relax/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.csv      (columns: t,B,M,S)

And a metadata JSON per run (derived physical parameters, Q, etc.):
    out_dir/meta/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.json

A manifest.csv at the top of out_dir summarizes all runs (one row
per run), to facilitate loading in pandas during analysis.

Usage
-----
    python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir /home/jps/sweep_results         --n_seeds 5 --grid_n 30 --quick_test 1

    --quick_test 1   runs a reduced version (fewer dampings/seeds,
                      short t_sim) just to validate that the pipeline
                      works end-to-end before the full campaign.
    --quick_test 0   runs the full campaign according to the script.

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --out_dir OUT_DIR
  --grid_n GRID_N       N=M of the grid (default 30 -> 900 needles)
  --n_seeds N_SEEDS
  --n_dampings N_DAMPINGS
  --Q_min Q_MIN
  --Q_max Q_MAX
  --geometries GEOMETRIES
  --R R
  --B_max_factor B_MAX_FACTOR
                        B_max = factor * B_ref (dipolar field between
                        neighbors), to ensure saturation at the peak of the
                        cycle
  --t_sim_periods T_SIM_PERIODS
                        t_sim in units of T0 = 2*pi/omega0 (natural scale).
                        Hysteresis cycle has 5 segments; this is the TOTAL
                        time of the cycle.
  --pbc PBC
  --use_gpu USE_GPU
  --skip_relax_stage SKIP_RELAX_STAGE
                        If 1, only runs Stage 1 (hysteresis), skips Stage 2
                        (relaxation/domains)
  --quick_test QUICK_TEST
                        If 1, overrides n_seeds=1, n_dampings=3,

43: import os
44: import sys
45: import json
46: import time
47: import argparse
48: import itertools
49: import numpy as np
50: 
51: sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
52: import compass as cs
53: 
54: 
55: # ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
56: # Fixed physical parameters of the study (same "tabletop" needle in all
57: # runs; only geometry/R/damping/seed vary)
58: # ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
59: R_DEFAULT          = 0.025      # m
60: NEEDLE_FRAC        = 0.80       # same CLI default
61: DT_FACTOR          = 0.05       # same CLI default
62: CUTOFF_DEFAULT     = 3.5        # same CLI default (in units of R)
63: NOISE_DEFAULT      = 1.5        # rad, initial noise in angles (default make_grid)
64: 
65: 
66: def derive_needle_geometry(R):
67:     needle_len   = NEEDLE_FRAC * 2.0 * R
68:     needle_width = needle_len * 0.22
69:     thickness    = cs.NEEDLE_THICKNESS_DEFAULT
70:     return needle_len, needle_width, thickness
71: 
72: 
73: def compute_physical_params(R):
74:     """Replicates exactly what main() does to derive inertia/moment
75:     from geometry, so that the study is physically consistent
76:     among the 3 geometries (same real needle, same steel density)."""
77:     needle_len, needle_width, thickness = derive_needle_geometry(R)
78:     inertia = cs.compute_inertia_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness)
79:     moment  = cs.compute_moment_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness)
80:     return inertia, moment, needle_len, needle_width, thickness
81: 
82: 
83: def compute_Q(inertia, moment, damping, r_nn):
84:     """Replicates the internal calculation of relax() for Q = omega0*I/b,
85:     using the dipolar B_ref between nearest neighbors as the scale field."""
86:     B_ref  = cs.MU0_OVER_4PI * 2.0 * moment / r_nn**3
87:     omega0 = np.sqrt(moment * B_ref / inertia)
88:     Q      = omega0 * inertia / damping if damping > 0 else np.inf
89:     return Q, omega0, B_ref
90: 
91: 
92: def make_damping_grid(inertia, moment, r_nn, n_points=8, Q_min=0.05, Q_max=15.0):
93:     """Constructs the damping grid log-spaced in Q, then converts to
94:     real `damping` values via the relation Q = omega0*I/b."""
95:     B_ref  = cs.MU0_OVER_4PI * 2.0 * moment / r_nn**3
96:     omega0 = np.sqrt(moment * B_ref / inertia)
97:     Q_vals = np.geomspace(Q_max, Q_min, n_points)   # from most underdamped to most overdamped
98:     damping_vals = omega0 * inertia / Q_vals
99:     return damping_vals, Q_vals, omega0
100: 
101: 
102: def run_one_hysteresis(geometry, R, damping, seed, t_sim, B_max, n_grid,
103:                         pbc=False, dt_factor=DT_FACTOR, use_gpu=False,
104:                         show_progress=False):
105:     np.random.seed(seed)
106:     inertia, moment, needle_len, needle_width, thickness = compute_physical_params(R)
107: 
108:     xs, ys, thetas, r_nn, Lx, Ly = cs.make_grid(
109:         N=n_grid, M=n_grid, geometry=geometry, noise=NOISE_DEFAULT, R=R)
110: 
111:     Q, omega0, B_ref = compute_Q(inertia, moment, damping, r_nn)
112: 
113:     phi_ext_deg = 0.0  # fixed field direction; symmetry axis chosen per geometry does not matter for M_proj
114: 
115:     t0 = time.perf_counter()
116:     theta_f, omega_f, hist, n_frames, dt, stop_reason, field_log = cs.relax(
117:         thetas, xs, ys,
118:         t_sim=t_sim, dt_factor=dt_factor,
119:         inertia=inertia, damping=damping,
120:         cutoff=CUTOFF_DEFAULT, ext_field=(B_max, 0.0),
121:         moment=moment, field_mode='hysteresis',
122:         pbc=pbc, Lx=Lx if pbc else None, Ly=Ly if pbc else None,
123:         use_gpu=use_gpu, show_progress=show_progress,
124:         make_images=False,
125:     )
126:     wall_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
127: 
128:     meta = dict(
129:         geometry=geometry, R=R, n_grid=n_grid, seed=seed,
130:         damping=damping, Q=Q, omega0=omega0, B_ref=B_ref, B_max=B_max,
131:         inertia=inertia, moment=moment, r_nn=r_nn,
132:         needle_len=needle_len, needle_width=needle_width, thickness=thickness,
133:         t_sim=t_sim, dt=dt, dt_factor=dt_factor, n_steps=len(field_log),
134:         pbc=pbc, stop_reason=stop_reason, wall_seconds=wall_s,
135:         field_mode='hysteresis',

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """
3: damping_sweepV02.py
4: ===================
5: 
6: Simulation campaign for the central study:
7:     "How does the damping coefficient control the shape of the
8:     hysteresis loop and the statistics of avalanches in classical dipolar
9:     lattices, and how does this depend on the geometry (square / triangular /
10:     honeycomb)?"
11: 
12: New in V02 (relative to V01):
13:     --n_workers N : executes N runs in parallel (independent processes;
14:                     nearly linear scaling with number of cores).
15:                     Each worker runs in its own working directory
16:                     to prevent collision of temporary files
17:                     (hysteresis_loop.csv) recorded by the simulator in
18:                     the current directory.
19:     incremental manifest : the manifest.csv is updated after EACH completed
20:                     run (not just at the end) — an interruption in the
21:                     middle of the campaign does not lose progress.
22:     --resume 1    : resumes an interrupted campaign — runs already
23:                     registered in manifest.csv are skipped.
24: 
25: This script DOES NOT modify compass.py. It imports the module and calls
26: relax() programmatically, sweeping:
27: 
28:     damping  x  seed  x  geometry
29: 
30: for the field mode 'hysteresis' (Stage 1) and 'static' B=0 (Stage 2,
31: free relaxation for domain statistics).
32: 
33: Output
34: ------
35: For each run, saves a CSV with the complete field_log:
36:     out_dir/hysteresis/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.csv
37:     out_dir/relax/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.csv      (columns: t,B,M,S)
38: 
39: And a metadata JSON per run (derived physical parameters, Q, etc.):
40:     out_dir/meta/<geom>_damp<idx>_seed<seed>.json
41: 
42: A manifest.csv at the top of out_dir summarizes all runs (one row
43: per run), updated incrementally.
44: 
45: Usage
46: -----
47:     python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir /home/jps/sweep_results \
48:         --n_seeds 5 --grid_n 30 --n_workers 8
49: 
50:     --quick_test 1   runs a reduced version (fewer dampings/seeds,
51:                       short t_sim) just to validate that the pipeline
52:                       works end-to-end before the full campaign.
53: """

69: # ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
70: # Fixed physical parameters of the study (same "tabletop" needle in all
71: # runs; only geometry/R/damping/seed vary)
72: # ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
73: R_DEFAULT          = 0.025      # m
74: NEEDLE_FRAC        = 0.80       # same CLI default
75: DT_FACTOR          = 0.05       # same CLI default
76: CUTOFF_DEFAULT     = 3.5        # same CLI default (in units of R)
77: NOISE_DEFAULT      = 1.5        # rad, initial noise in angles (default make_grid)
78: 
79: 
80: def derive_needle_geometry(R):
81:     needle_len   = NEEDLE_FRAC * 2.0 * R
82:     needle_width = needle_len * 0.22
83:     thickness    = cs.NEEDLE_THICKNESS_DEFAULT
84:     return needle_len, needle_width, thickness
85: 
86: 
87: def compute_physical_params(R):
88:     """Replicates exactly what main() does to derive inertia/moment
89:     from geometry, so that the study is physically consistent
90:     among the 3 geometries (same real needle, same steel density)."""
91:     needle_len, needle_width, thickness = derive_needle_geometry(R)
92:     inertia = cs.compute_inertia_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness)
93:     moment  = cs.compute_moment_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness)
94:     return inertia, moment, needle_len, needle_width, thickness
95: 
96: 
97: def compute_Q(inertia, moment, damping, r_nn):
98:     """Replicates the internal calculation of relax() for Q = omega0*I/b,
99:     using the dipolar B_ref between nearest neighbors as the scale field."""
100:     B_ref  = cs.MU0_OVER_4PI * 2.0 * moment / r_nn**3
101:     omega0 = np.sqrt(moment * B_ref / inertia)
102:     Q      = omega0 * inertia / damping if damping > 0 else np.inf
103:     return Q, omega0, B_ref
104: 
105: 
106: def make_damping_grid(inertia, moment, r_nn, n_points=8, Q_min=0.05, Q_max=15.0):
107:     """Constructs the damping grid log-spaced in Q, then converts to
108:     real `damping` values via the relation Q = omega0*I/b."""
109:     B_ref  = cs.MU0_OVER_4PI * 2.0 * moment / r_nn**3
110:     omega0 = np.sqrt(moment * B_ref / inertia)
111:     Q_vals = np.geomspace(Q_max, Q_min, n_points)   # from most underdamped to most overdamped
112:     damping_vals = omega0 * inertia / Q_vals
113:     return damping_vals, Q_vals, omega0
114: 
115: 
116: def run_one_hysteresis(geometry, R, damping, seed, t_sim, B_max, n_grid,
117:                         pbc=False, dt_factor=DT_FACTOR, use_gpu=False,
118:                         show_progress=False):
119:     np.random.seed(seed)
120:     inertia, moment, needle_len, needle_width, thickness = compute_physical_params(R)
121: 
122:     xs, ys, thetas, r_nn, Lx, Ly = cs.make_grid(
123:         N=n_grid, M=n_grid, geometry=geometry, noise=NOISE_DEFAULT, R=R)
124: 
125:     Q, omega0, B_ref = compute_Q(inertia, moment, damping, r_nn)
126: 
127:     phi_ext_deg = 0.0  # fixed field direction; symmetry axis chosen per geometry does not matter for M_proj
128: 
129:     t0 = time.perf_counter()
130:     theta_f, omega_f, hist, n_frames, dt, stop_reason, field_log = cs.relax(
131:         thetas, xs, ys,
132:         t_sim=t_sim, dt_factor=dt_factor,
133:         inertia=inertia, damping=damping,
134:         cutoff=CUTOFF_DEFAULT, ext_field=(B_max, 0.0),
135:         moment=moment, field_mode='hysteresis',
136:         pbc=pbc, Lx=Lx if pbc else None, Ly=Ly if pbc else None,
137:         use_gpu=use_gpu, show_progress=show_progress,
138:         make_images=False,
139:     )
140:     wall_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
141: 
142:     meta = dict(
143:         geometry=geometry, R=R, n_grid=n_grid, seed=seed,
144:         damping=damping, Q=Q, omega0=omega0, B_ref=B_ref, B_max=B_max,
145:         inertia=inertia, moment=moment, r_nn=r_nn,
146:         needle_len=needle_len, needle_width=needle_width, thickness=thickness,
147:         t_sim=t_sim, dt=dt, dt_factor=dt_factor, n_steps=len(field_log),
148:         pbc=pbc, stop_reason=stop_reason, wall_seconds=wall_s,
149:         field_mode='hysteresis',
150:     )
151:     return field_log, meta
152: 
153: 
154: def run_one_relax(geometry, R, damping, seed, t_sim, n_grid,
155:                    pbc=False, dt_factor=DT_FACTOR, use_gpu=False,
156:                    show_progress=False):
157:     np.random.seed(seed)
158:     inertia, moment, needle_len, needle_width, thickness = compute_physical_params(R)
159: 
160:     xs, ys, thetas, r_nn, Lx, Ly = cs.make_grid(
161:         N=n_grid, M=n_grid, geometry=geometry, noise=NOISE_DEFAULT, R=R)
162: 
163:     Q, omega0, B_ref = compute_Q(inertia, moment, damping, r_nn)
164: 
165:     t0 = time.perf_counter()
166:     theta_f, omega_f, hist, n_frames, dt, stop_reason, field_log = cs.relax(
167:         thetas, xs, ys,
168:         t_sim=t_sim, dt_factor=dt_factor,
169:         inertia=inertia, damping=damping,
170:         cutoff=CUTOFF_DEFAULT, ext_field=(0.0, 0.0),
171:         moment=moment, field_mode='static',
172:         pbc=pbc, Lx=Lx if pbc else None, Ly=Ly if pbc else None,
173:         use_gpu=use_gpu, show_progress=show_progress,
174:         make_images=False,
175:     )
176:     wall_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
177: 
178:     # domain statistics in final state
179:     domain_labels, n_domains = cs.label_magnetic_domains(theta_f, tol_deg=15.0)
180:     sizes = np.bincount(domain_labels.ravel())
181:     sizes = sizes[sizes > 0]
182: 
183:     meta = dict(
184:         geometry=geometry, R=R, n_grid=n_grid, seed=seed,
185:         damping=damping, Q=Q, omega0=omega0, B_ref=B_ref,
186:         inertia=inertia, moment=moment, r_nn=r_nn,
187:         needle_len=needle_len, needle_width=needle_width, thickness=thickness,
188:         t_sim=t_sim, dt=dt, dt_factor=dt_factor, n_steps=len(field_log),
189:         pbc=pbc, stop_reason=stop_reason, wall_seconds=wall_s,
190:         field_mode='static_relax',
191:         n_domains=int(n_domains),
192:         domain_sizes=sizes.tolist(),
193:     )
194:     return field_log, meta
195:

197: def save_field_log_csv(field_log, path):
198:     arr = np.array(field_log)  # columns: t, B, M, S
199:     header = "t,B,M,S"
200:     np.savetxt(path, arr, delimiter=",", header=header, comments="")

Instead, they are responsible only for orchestrating the sweep campaign by running the simulations and outputting raw data:
- CSV log files (`field_log` containing columns `t, B, M, S`)
- JSON metadata files (containing physical parameters like calculated inertia, moments, and quality factor $Q$)
- A consolidated `manifest.csv` table listing all runs

def derive_needle_geometry(R, needle_frac=0.80, needle_thickness=0.0004):
    needle_len   = needle_frac * 2.0 * R
    needle_width = needle_len * 0.22
    thickness    = needle_thickness
    return needle_len, needle_width, thickness


def compute_physical_params(R, needle_frac=0.80, needle_thickness=0.0004,
                            steel_density=7850.0, steel_Bsat=None,
                            moment=None, inertia=None):
    """Replicates exactly what main() does to derive inertia/moment
    from geometry, so that the study is physically consistent
    among the 3 geometries (same real needle, same steel density)."""
    needle_len, needle_width, thickness = derive_needle_geometry(R, needle_frac, needle_thickness)
    if inertia is None:
        inertia_val = cs.compute_inertia_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness, density=steel_density)
    else:
        inertia_val = inertia

    if moment is None:
        ms_used = steel_Bsat / (4.0 * np.pi * 1e-7) if steel_Bsat is not None else cs.STEEL_MS_SATURATION_DEFAULT
        moment_val = cs.compute_moment_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness, Ms=ms_used)
    else:
        moment_val = moment

    return inertia_val, moment_val, needle_len, needle_width, thickness

You should choose **`damping_sweep.py`** (sequential execution) over **`damping_sweepV02.py`** (parallel execution) in the following scenarios:

### 1. When Using GPU Acceleration (`--use_gpu 1`)
If you configure the sweep to run on the GPU (e.g., using CUDA/CuPy), running multiple simulations in parallel will lead to **GPU memory contention and resource bottlenecks**. Spawning concurrent processes trying to allocate GPU tensors simultaneously can lead to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors or overall slower execution. 
* *Rule of thumb*: Use the sequential `damping_sweep.py` for GPU sweeps, and the parallel `damping_sweepV02.py` for CPU sweeps.

### 2. For Step-by-Step Debugging and Console Logging
Since `damping_sweepV02.py` runs multiple processes simultaneously, their console outputs, warning logs, and error messages are interleaved, making them hard to read.
* If you are troubleshooting a script error, testing custom physical parameters, or want to read clean output logs for a single run in real-time, `damping_sweep.py` makes it much easier to inspect stdout step-by-step.

### 3. On Low-Resource Systems
If you are running the script on a machine with a single core or very limited RAM:
* The overhead of spawning separate worker processes, creating scratch folders, and managing concurrent execution in `damping_sweepV02.py` is unnecessary. `damping_sweep.py` has a lower memory and process footprint.

The "insufficient to fit" message appears when the analysis script detects **fewer than 20 total avalanches** for a given configuration (aggregated across all seeds). Because a power-law maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) fit is statistically invalid with too few data points, the script reports this message rather than printing a spurious result.

Here is how you can resolve this:

### 1. Lower the Avalanche Detection Threshold (Easiest)
By default, the analysis script filters out small jumps by using an avalanche detection threshold of `4.0` times the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) of the field derivative. You can lower this threshold to make the detector more sensitive, which captures more (smaller) avalanches:
```bash
python3 damping_sweep_analysis.py \
    --sweep_dir results_noise \
    --out_dir results_noise/analysis \
    --mad_threshold 2.0
```
*Try lowering `--mad_threshold` to `2.0` or `1.5` to increase the count of detected avalanches.*

---

### 2. Turn off `--quick_test`
If you ran the sweep with `--quick_test 1` to test the code, the simulation duration `t_sim` is set to be very short, and the lattice is small ($12\times12$). This naturally limits the number of avalanche events. Make sure you run the actual campaign (or a pilot) with `--quick_test 0` (default) so that it runs the full hysteresis cycle.

---

### 3. Increase the Lattice Grid Size (`--grid_n`)
Small lattices do not have enough discrete needles to trigger large avalanche statistics. If you are running at `12\times12` or `20\times20`, consider increasing it to `30\times30` (900 needles) or `40\times40` (1600 needles). The number of detected avalanches grows exponentially with the array size.

---

### 4. Increase the Number of Seeds (`--n_seeds`)
Since the analysis script aggregates all avalanches from all seed runs for each `(geometry, Q)` point before performing the fit, increasing `--n_seeds` from `3` to `5` or `10` will directly multiply the number of sample points available for the MLE fit.

Here is a recommended configuration for a **massive campaign (720 simulations total)** that will complete in **5--10 minutes** using CPU parallelization:

### Step 1: Run the Massive Sweep Campaign
This command runs a $30\times30$ array (900 needles) sweeping 12 quality factors (fine resolution) with 10 seeds per geometry, adding $0.3$ damping noise, and utilizing 8 CPU cores:

```bash
python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir "$(pwd)/results_massive" \
    --grid_n 30 \
    --n_dampings 12 \
    --n_seeds 10 \
    --damping_noise 0.3 \
    --n_workers 8
```

#### Why these parameters are chosen for a massive run:
* **`--grid_n 30`** ($30\times30 = 900$ needles): Large enough to establish clear magnetic domains and long avalanche cascades, while keeping simulation times short (~3.5 seconds per run). If your machine has high specs and you want to scale higher, you can use **`--grid_n 40`** (1600 needles).
* **`--n_dampings 12`**: Increases the resolution of the curves, mapping out the transition from underdamped to overdamped regimes with 12 distinct points instead of the default 8.
* **`--n_seeds 10`**: Running 10 different random noise realizations (seeds) per point provides a large sample size ($N_{\text{total}}$) of avalanche events, reducing standard errors on the MLE fits (exponent $\tau$).
* **`--n_workers 8`**: Distributes the 720 runs across 8 parallel worker processes.

---

### Step 2: Run the High-Precision Analysis
Once completed, analyze the campaign. Since the sample size is large, you can keep the default MAD threshold for highly selective avalanche detection:

```bash
python3 damping_sweep_analysis.py \
    --sweep_dir results_massive \
    --out_dir results_massive/analysis
```

This will output the summary CSV files and generate the publication plots with high resolution and minimal error bars.

173: \subsection{Incremental Manifest \& Resume Support}
174: Unlike the serial version which writes the manifest at the end, V02 updates \texttt{manifest.csv} incrementally after \textbf{each completed run} and flushes it immediately. 
175: If the campaign is aborted (due to power loss, user interrupt, etc.), it can be resumed by passing \texttt{--resume 1}. The script checks the existing manifest, identifies which jobs are already completed, and skips them automatically.
176: 
177: \subsection{CLI Additions in V02}
178: In addition to all the parameters of the serial version, V02 supports:
179: \begin{itemize}
180:     \item \texttt{--n\_workers} (Default: 1): Number of processes to run in parallel.
181:     \item \texttt{--resume} (Default: 0): Set to 1 to resume a previously interrupted run in the same directory.
182: \end{itemize}
183: 
184: % ======================================================================
185: \section{\texttt{damping\_sweep\_analysis.py} (Post-Processing)}
186: \label{sec:damping_analysis}
187: % ======================================================================
188: 
189: The script \texttt{damping\_sweep\_analysis.py} processes the data directory generated by either of the sweep scripts. 
190: 
191: \subsection{Hysteresis Metric Extraction}
192: For each Stage 1 hysteresis run, the script calculates:
193: \begin{itemize}
194:     \item \textbf{Loop Area}: Computed using Green's theorem to evaluate the closed-line integral $\oint M(B) dB$. It measures the energy dissipated per cycle.
195:     \item \textbf{Coercive Field} ($B_c$): Estimated by linear interpolation of the field $B$ when magnetization crosses zero ($M = 0$).
196:     \item \textbf{Remanent Magnetization} ($M_r$): Estimated by linear interpolation of the magnetization $M$ when the external field crosses zero ($B = 0$).

\subsection*{B.10 --- Full scientific campaign (satellite scripts)}

The simulation campaign sweep scripts are designed to run programmatic sweeps over multiple values of damping (friction), initial seeds (noise realizations), and lattice geometries to generate statistical datasets for hysteresis loop shape and avalanche scaling analysis. 

These scripts import from the core simulation file (\code{compass.py}) and call the simulator API (\code{relax()}) directly. Both \code{damping\_sweep.py} and \code{damping\_sweepV02.py} have been adapted to accept all major simulation parameters of \code{compass.py}, including geometry options (\code{--needle\_frac}, \code{--needle\_thickness}, \code{--steel\_density}, \code{--steel\_Bsat}, \code{--moment}, \code{--inertia}), integration parameters (\code{--dt\_factor}, \code{--noise}), domain clustering parameters (\code{--domain\_tol}), and per-needle random damping noise (\code{--damping\_noise}).

\subsubsection*{1. Serial Campaign Execution (\code{damping\_sweep.py})}
The \code{damping\_sweep.py} script executes a serial sweep across geometries, seeds, and damping coefficients. It performs Stage 1 (hysteresis) followed by Stage 2 (field-free relaxation for domain statistics).

\begin{verbatim}
# Quick test to validate the pipeline (low resolution, short runtime):
python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir results_quick --quick_test 1

# Full campaign with damping noise and custom integration time steps:
python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir results_campaign \
    --grid_n 30 --n_seeds 5 --n_dampings 8 \
    --Q_min 0.05 --Q_max 15.0 --geometries square,triangular,honeycomb \
    --damping_noise 0.3 --dt_factor 0.05
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection*{2. Parallelized Execution with Resume Capability (\code{damping\_sweepV02.py})}
The parallelized version \code{damping\_sweepV02.py} parallelizes execution using a Python \code{ProcessPoolExecutor}. To prevent temporary files (\code{hysteresis\_loop.csv}) from colliding between workers, each process runs in its own dynamic scratch directory. A manifest (\code{manifest.csv}) tracks the completion status of each run, enabling resumption if the campaign is interrupted.

\begin{verbatim}
# Run the campaign parallelized across 8 cores:
python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir results_parallel \
    --grid_n 30 --n_seeds 5 --n_dampings 8 --n_workers 8 \
    --damping_noise 0.3 --dt_factor 0.05

# Resume an interrupted campaign (automatically skips already completed runs):
python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir results_parallel \
    --grid_n 30 --n_seeds 5 --n_dampings 8 --n_workers 8 --resume 1
\end{verbatim}

38: \begin{abstract}
39: \noindent
40: This report documents the full development of the \code{compass\_sim} project: a Python simulator for two-dimensional arrays of magnetic compass needles interacting through complete dipolar coupling, with inertial Newtonian dynamics in SI units. The project began as a pedagogical demonstration of the analogy between compass arrays and magnetic materials, including hysteresis and domain formation, and evolved over six development sessions into a research instrument with publication potential. The report records the project decisions, problems encountered and solutions adopted, the code-version history (V20--V66), the research and publication strategy built around a gap identified in the literature, and the results of the pilot campaign on ``damping~$\times$~hysteresis/avalanches''. The pilot already shows the central signal sought: a systematic increase of the avalanche exponent $\tau$ with the quality factor $Q$.
41: \end{abstract}
42: 
43: \tableofcontents
44: \newpage
45: 
46: % ======================================================================
47: \section{Project objective}
48: % ======================================================================
49: 
50: The project now has two layered objectives, reflecting its historical evolution.
51: 
52: \paragraph{Original objective (pedagogical/demonstrative).}
53: To build a visual simulation of an array of compass needles that rotate only under the magnetic field generated by each needle on its neighbors, seeking the collective directional equilibrium. The simulation provides a direct and intuitive mechanical analogy with real magnetic materials, capable of displaying hysteretic behavior and magnetic-domain formation from a top view and exportable as video.
54: 
55: \paragraph{Current objective (scientific).}
56: To use the simulator, which implements real Newtonian \emph{inertial} dynamics, a rare feature in this literature, to address a nonequilibrium statistical-physics question with publication potential:
57: 
58: \begin{quote}\itshape
59: Does the damping coefficient control the universality class of avalanches and the shape of the hysteresis loop in classical dipolar arrays with long-range and anisotropic coupling? Does this response depend on the lattice geometry (square, triangular, honeycomb), that is, on geometric frustration?
60: \end{quote}

V36 & Parameter \code{--progress\_bar} \{0,1\}. \\

V39 & Parameter \code{--make\_images} \{0,1\}: suppresses all PNG generation while preserving CSVs; $\sim 3\times$ speedup in small arrays. \\
V40 & Precomputed dipolar-interaction tensor: matrix--vector products (BLAS/cuBLAS) per step; measured speedup of \textbf{35--45$\times$}; validation to machine \emph{epsilon}; memory protection with automatic fallback. \\

Legacy modes bit-identical to V40. \\
V42 & Parameter \code{--t\_sim\_full} \{0,1\}: with 1, the simulation runs until the end of \code{t\_sim}, disabling all physical early stops ($S{=}1.00$, rest, torque equilibrium), useful for uniform-length time series in sweeps. Ctrl+I and Ctrl+C remain active; default (0) bit-identical to V41. \\
V43 & User-reported fix: the comparison figure did not draw halos in any mode. Halo logic was extracted to \code{draw\_halos\_batch()} and applied to both comparison panels, with domain count in each panel title in \code{domains} mode. Also corrected the comparison supertitle, which displayed ``B\_ext=0.00'' for mT fields. \code{plot\_state} figures are pixel-identical and physics is bit-identical to V42. \\
V44 & Two-line live progress panel: bar and periodic status are rewritten in place using ANSI codes with a cursor invariant, eliminating terminal line stacking. TTY detection preserves log behavior without escape codes for redirected output. Validated with \code{pyte}; final screen with exactly one bar line and one status line; clean interleaved phase-transition messages; bit-identical physics. \\
V45 & Hysteresis-mode video with dual panel: needles on the left and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time on the right, with the current point highlighted. Other video modes unchanged; bit-identical physics. \\
V46 & Alignment of help-text frames in the \emph{docstring}: right borders of parameter boxes, which meandered in plain-text editors because of visual-width differences (accented characters, arrows, \emph{box-drawing}), were normalized to uniform visual width; three long descriptions were slightly shortened to fit. No effect on physics or execution. \\
V47 & Autoscale in the $M\times H$ hysteresis curve: added parameter \code{--hyst\_autoscale} to dynamically scale the axes in both the live simulation frames (dual panel) and the final hysteresis plots, based on the accumulated minimum and maximum fields and magnetization. Translated all new comments and help texts to English. \\
V48 & Bugfix and parameter adjustment: resolved a syntax error on \code{box\_w} assignment in the screen indicators; changed the parameter \code{--hyst\_autoscale} to accept integers \code{0} and \code{1} (with default \code{0}) instead of a boolean flag. \\
V49 & Parameter and visualization refinement: resolved overlap between HUD boxes and the top row of needles by dynamically reserving the top 20\% of the vertical space; adjusted the field indicator bar to accept and represent signed values, ranging from $-B_{\max}$ (empty) to $+B_{\max}$ (full), with the center (half-full) representing zero field; updated the box arrow to rotate by $180^\circ$ for negative fields. \\
V50 & Progress bar translation and English layout: reorganized the terminal output progress tracking to a clean 3-line print format using standard English labels (`Integrating`, `step`, `steps/s`) to display runtime physics parameters and step counts in real time. \\
V51 & Legend layout alignment: vertically aligned the top edges of the time and external field HUD boxes; redesigned the field arrow to have a constant length and placed it inside the field box at the top right (adjacent to the label), ensuring visibility even at very small fields. \\
V52 & English translation: fully translated all remaining Portuguese console/terminal logs printed during initialization, physical parameters display, and simulation completion to English. \\
V53 & Circular direction dial and sign indicator: added a circular direction dial at the top right of the external field box and a sign indicator arrow next to the horizontal field intensity bar at the bottom right. \\
V54 & Developer metadata in terminal log: added code version and developer name to the simulation initialization banner. \\
V55 & HUD direction dial arrow scaling: scaled the arrow length within the circular dial proportionally to the normalized field intensity ($[-1, +1]$ relative to maximum field) and removed the bottom-right sign indicator arrow. \\
V56 & HUD direction dial arrow scaling minimum length calibration: defined a minimum arrow length ($0.35 R_{\mathrm{dial}}$) for active fields so that the shaft remains longer than the arrowhead at small fields, reaching full radius ($1.0 R_{\mathrm{dial}}$) at maximum field. \\
V57 & HUD direction dial bold arrow: replaced the thin \code{annotate} arrow in the circular direction dial with a bold, filled \code{FancyArrow} patch (wide rectangular shaft and large triangular head, filled with the field color and dark outline), matching the visual style of a road-sign directional indicator. \\
V58 & HUD direction dial bold arrow homothetic scaling: scaled the width, head width, and head length proportionally to the field intensity to preserve the arrow's aspect ratio (avoiding stubby rendering) as the field is reduced and inverted. \\
V59 & Random per-needle damping noise: added \code{--damping\_noise} parameter to introduce random variations in friction/damping for each individual needle, simulating realistic pivot differences. \\
V60 & Command-line interface translation: fully translated all remaining Portuguese help strings, warning messages, and parameter options in the program parser to English. \\
V61 & Section 4 plot string translation: translated all remaining Portuguese label, axis, and title strings in the hysteresis and sinusoidal plotting functions to English. \\
V62 & Visual warnings translation: translated the warning message printed when suppression of summary PNG images is enabled with `--make\_images 0` to English. \\
V63 & Performance optimizations and translations: optimized the Verlet integration loop by pre-computing integration constants and passing explicit array-library backend references, and translated all remaining Portuguese log descriptions and labels in \code{relax()} to English. \\
V64 & Alignment of sweep files: corrected the import references in all campaign sweep files (\code{damping\_sweep.py}, \code{damping\_sweepV02.py}, and \code{sweep\_damping\_hysteresis.py}) to import from the latest optimized simulation file (\code{compass.py}) rather than the outdated \code{compass\_sim.py}. \\
V65 & Translation of sweep scripts: fully translated all comments, help text, parameters, and log string outputs in all campaign sweep files to English. \\
V66 & HUD external field intensity bar update: redesigned the horizontal field bar to grow bidirectionally from center (left for negative fields, right for positive fields, zero at zero field, with a central red zero-reference line). \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\emph{Satellite scripts (own version record):}} \\
\code{damping\_sweep} V01 & orchestration of the damping~$\times$~seed~$\times$~geometry campaign. \\
\code{damping\_sweep} V02 & parallel execution (\code{--n\_workers}), incremental \emph{manifest}, and resume (\code{--resume}). \\
\code{damping\_sweep\_analysis.py} & loop metrics, avalanche detection, MLE power-law fitting, plots. \\
\end{longtable}

To run the GPU-accelerated version of the sweep campaign, you should pass the **`--use_gpu 1`** flag. 

Importantly, to prevent GPU memory allocation collisions and core contention, you should run the sweep **sequentially** (one simulation at a time on the GPU). 

Here are the commands for both scripts:

### Option A: Using the Serial Script (Recommended for GPU)
```bash
python3 damping_sweep.py --out_dir results_gpu --use_gpu 1 --grid_n 30
```

### Option B: Using the Parallel Script (Restricted to 1 worker)
If you want to use the V02 script (for instance, to take advantage of its incremental manifest saving and resume features), you can still use it, but you **must set `--n_workers 1`** to avoid launching concurrent jobs on the same GPU:
```bash
python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir "$(pwd)/results_parallel_gpu" \
    --use_gpu 1 \
    --n_workers 1 \
    --grid_n 30
```

### 1. Scientific Inferences from the Results

#### A. Hysteresis Loop Area and Coercivity ($B_c$)
* **Viscous Drag Domination**: In the highly overdamped regime ($Q \ll 1$), both loop area and coercivity increase sharply. This is expected: high viscosity ($b$) acts as a strong frictional lag, delaying the response of the needles to the changing external field. The loop is widened dynamically.
* **Plateau and Inertial Crossover**: For $Q > 1$ (underdamped), the loop area and coercivity level off, showing that once damping is sufficiently low, the dynamic delay is no longer dominated by viscosity but rather by the intrinsic inertia of the needles and dipolar interaction timescales. 
* **Dynamic Non-Monotonicity**: In the loop area plot, a subtle local minimum is visible around $Q \approx 3$ to $5$ before a slight rise at $Q = 15$. This is a classic signature of **inertial resonance**: under low damping, needles can overshoot their local equilibrium, leading to transient ringing that dissipates extra energy, slightly widening the loop.
* **Geometric Stability**: Across all damping regimes, the **triangular lattice** (red) exhibits the highest coercivity and loop area, followed by the **square lattice** (blue), while the **honeycomb lattice** (green) has the lowest. This suggests the triangular array forms the most stable collective magnetic configurations (highest energy barriers to flip).

#### B. Domain Size and Number Statistics
* **Triangular Array Coarsening**: The triangular lattice shows a clean, monotonic increase in mean domain size (from $\approx 5$ to $\approx 15$ needles) and a corresponding drop in domain count as $Q$ increases. **Interpretation**: Lower damping (higher $Q$) gives the needles more kinetic energy to swing past shallow local energy barriers during relaxation, enabling the system to organize into larger, co-aligned domains.
* **Square and Honeycomb Gridlock**: In stark contrast, both square and honeycomb lattices remain completely locked in a highly fragmented micro-domain state (mean size $\approx 1.5$ needles, with $\approx 450$--$700$ domains) across the entire range of $Q$. **Interpretation**: Their dipolar interactions create highly degenerate, frustrated energy landscapes with deep, localized energy minima. Viscous damping relaxation alone is insufficient to allow these lattices to coarsen.

#### C. Remanence ($M_r$)
* **Frustration and Decay**: The remanence of triangular and square lattices remains high ($M_r > 0.9$) across all Q values. However, the **honeycomb lattice** shows a dramatic drop in remanence for $Q > 1$, falling to $M_r \approx 0.68$ at $Q = 15$. 
* **Interpretation**: Honeycomb arrays have high coordinate frustration. Under low damping (high inertia), the needles easily escape the metastable magnetized state at $B=0$ and relax into lower-energy demagnetized configurations.

---

### 2. Next Steps for the Research Plan

To build a publication-grade paper from these findings, the following next steps are recommended:

1. **Analyze the Avalanche Exponent $\tau(Q)$ (The Central Physics Test)**:
   * We need to inspect the `tau_vs_Q.png` plot. Check if the power-law exponent $\tau$ of the avalanche sizes undergoes a systematic crossover between the overdamped ($Q \ll 1$) and underdamped ($Q \gg 1$) regimes, and whether this crossover is geometry-dependent.
2. **Verify Finite-Size and Boundary Effects on Domain Locking**:
   * Since the square and honeycomb arrays are locked in extremely small domain sizes ($\approx 1.5$ needles), we must verify whether this is a boundary-induced effect.
   * **Action**: Run a focused set of sweeps with **Periodic Boundary Conditions (`--pbc 1`)** and a larger lattice size (e.g., `--grid_n 40` or `50`) to see if square and honeycomb arrays are still locked or if they begin to coarsen when boundary constraints are removed.
3. **Finite-Time Sweep Rate Convergence**:
   * In a real experiment, hysteresis metrics depend on the sweep rate of the external field. Verify that the loop metrics converge by running a few test configurations with a longer sweep duration (`--t_sim_periods 80` instead of `40`) to ensure the results represent the quasi-static limit.
4. **Energy Barrier Mapping (Satellite Code)**:

I have implemented the **FORC (First-Order Reversal Curve)** method in [compass.py](file:///Users/jps/Dropbox/simula%20agulhas/compass.py) as a new `field_mode` option. 

### Implementation Details:

1. **New Field Mode Choice**:
   Added `'forc'` to the choices of `--field_mode`.
   
2. **Additional CLI Parameters**:
   * **`--forc_Br`**: The reversal field $B_r$ in Tesla (Default: `0.0` T). This is the field value where the ramp changes direction and sweeps back.
   * **`--forc_t_sat`**: Duration of the positive saturation phase in seconds (Default: `0.2 * t_sim`).
   * **`--forc_t_rev`**: The time in seconds when the reversal point $B_r$ is reached and the field begins rising back to saturation (Default: `0.5 * t_sim`).

3. **Field Profile Logic (`relax()`)**:
   Under `field_mode == 'forc'`, the external field $B_{\text{ext}}(t)$ follows a 3-segment schedule:
   * **Segment 1 (Saturation)**: $t \le t_{\text{sat}} \longrightarrow B_{\text{ext}} = B_{\max}$ (maintains positive saturation).
   * **Segment 2 (Ramp Down)**: $t_{\text{sat}} < t \le t_{\text{rev}} \longrightarrow B_{\text{ext}}$ ramps down linearly from $B_{\max}$ to the reversal field $B_r$.
   * **Segment 3 (Ramp Up/Measurement)**: $t_{\text{rev}} < t \le t_{\text{sim}} \longrightarrow B_{\text{ext}}$ ramps linearly back up from $B_r$ to $B_{\max}$.

4. **Integration with Logging & Live Plotting**:
   * Reused the logging system so that it collects and outputs the reversal curve coordinates to **`forc_curve.csv`** at the end of the simulation.
   * Reused the live rendering frame logic: running `forc` mode with video export enabled will render a **dual-panel video** in real time (needles on the left, $M \times H$ minor reversal loop curve growing on the right).

### Example Command to Run a FORC Curve Simulation:
```bash
python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode forc \
    --ext_Bx 0.005 --forc_Br -0.002 --t_sim 4.0
```
*(This saturates the array at $+5$ mT, ramps it down to a reversal field of $-2$ mT, and sweeps it back to $+5$ mT, saving the raw curve details to `forc_curve.csv`).*

38: \begin{abstract}
39: \noindent
40: This report documents the full development of the \code{compass\_sim} project: a Python simulator for two-dimensional arrays of magnetic compass needles interacting through complete dipolar coupling, with inertial Newtonian dynamics in SI units. The project began as a pedagogical demonstration of the analogy between compass arrays and magnetic materials, including hysteresis and domain formation, and evolved over six development sessions into a research instrument with publication potential. The report records the project decisions, problems encountered and solutions adopted, the code-version history (V20--V66), the research and publication strategy built around a gap identified in the literature, and the results of the pilot campaign on ``damping~$\times$~hysteresis/avalanches''. The pilot already shows the central signal sought: a systematic increase of the avalanche exponent $\tau$ with the quality factor $Q$.

102: \paragraph{Simulator capabilities (current state, V66).}
103: The simulator supports three lattice geometries (square, triangular, honeycomb); \textbf{six} external-field modes: static; pulse with explicit timing (delay $\Delta t$ $\to$ field for $t_{\mathrm{pulse}}$ $\to$ zero field until equilibrium, with the legacy saturation/plateau criterion if $t_{\mathrm{pulse}}$ is not given); five-segment hysteresis ($0 \to +B \to 0 \to -B \to 0 \to +B$) with linear or log-symmetric spacing; sinusoidal field; and step modes \code{step\_pos} ($B{=}0$ for $\Delta t$, then field kept on) and \code{step\_neg} (field from $t{=}0$, removed at $\Delta t$). It also supports periodic boundary conditions with lattice images; real-time monitoring of the alignment order parameter $S \in [0,1]$; a real-equilibrium criterion (small angular velocity \emph{and} small mean torque) for pulse/step modes; optional GPU backend through CuPy; MP4 video export, summary images, and CSV time series $(t, B, M, S)$; magnetic-domain visualization through halo coloring; a precomputed dipolar tensor (V40); and performance instrumentation.

701: V25--V28 & GPU support via CuPy; \code{--gpu} flag; utilization investigation; performance instrumentation (throughput, ms/step). \\
702: V29--V33 & PBC with structure images in the dipolar field (default one copy); progress bar; automatic moment of inertia from real geometry (\SI{0.4}{mm} steel); Ctrl+C aborts immediately / Ctrl+I saves and exits (code 130). \\

704: V35 & Matplotlib rendering optimization through vectorized collections: 17--30$\times$ speedup; bitwise validation of geometry and physics. \\

708: V39 & Parameter \code{--make\_images} \{0,1\}: suppresses all PNG generation while preserving CSVs; $\sim 3\times$ speedup in small arrays. \\
709: V40 & Precomputed dipolar-interaction tensor: matrix--vector products (BLAS/cuBLAS) per step; measured speedup of \textbf{35--45$\times$}; validation to machine \emph{epsilon}; memory protection with automatic fallback. \\
710: V41 & New field protocols: hysteresis with log-symmetric spacing (\code{--hyst\_spacing log}, $\sim$15$\times$ finer sampling near $B{=}0$ for $k{=}5$); pulse with explicit timing (\code{--field\_delay}, \code{--t\_pulse}) and torque-equilibrium criterion (\code{--torque\_tol}); step modes \code{step\_pos}/\code{step\_neg}. Legacy modes bit-identical to V40. \\
711: V42 & Parameter \code{--t\_sim\_full} \{0,1\}: with 1, the simulation runs until the end of \code{t\_sim}, disabling all physical early stops ($S{=}1.00$, rest, torque equilibrium), useful for uniform-length time series in sweeps. Ctrl+I and Ctrl+C remain active; default (0) bit-identical to V41. \\
712: V43 & User-reported fix: the comparison figure did not draw halos in any mode. Halo logic was extracted to \code{draw\_halos\_batch()} and applied to both comparison panels, with domain count in each panel title in \code{domains} mode. Also corrected the comparison supertitle, which displayed ``B\_ext=0.00'' for mT fields. \code{plot\_state} figures are pixel-identical and physics is bit-identical to V42. \\
713: V44 & Two-line live progress panel: bar and periodic status are rewritten in place using ANSI codes with a cursor invariant, eliminating terminal line stacking. TTY detection preserves log behavior without escape codes for redirected output. Validated with \code{pyte}; final screen with exactly one bar line and one status line; clean interleaved phase-transition messages; bit-identical physics. \\
714: V45 & Hysteresis-mode video with dual panel: needles on the left and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time on the right, with the current point highlighted. Other video modes unchanged; bit-identical physics. \\
715: V46 & Alignment of help-text frames in the \emph{docstring}: right borders of parameter boxes, which meandered in plain-text editors because of visual-width differences (accented characters, arrows, \emph{box-drawing}), were normalized to uniform visual width; three long descriptions were slightly shortened to fit. No effect on physics or execution. \\
716: V47 & Autoscale in the $M\times H$ hysteresis curve: added parameter \code{--hyst\_autoscale} to dynamically scale the axes in both the live simulation frames (dual panel) and the final hysteresis plots, based on the accumulated minimum and maximum fields and magnetization. Translated all new comments and help texts to English. \\
717: V48 & Bugfix and parameter adjustment: resolved a syntax error on \code{box\_w} assignment in the screen indicators; changed the parameter \code{--hyst\_autoscale} to accept integers \code{0} and \code{1} (with default \code{0}) instead of a boolean flag. \\
718: V49 & Parameter and visualization refinement: resolved overlap between HUD boxes and the top row of needles by dynamically reserving the top 20\% of the vertical space; adjusted the field indicator bar to accept and represent signed values, ranging from $-B_{\max}$ (empty) to $+B_{\max}$ (full), with the center (half-full) representing zero field; updated the box arrow to rotate by $180^\circ$ for negative fields. \\
719: V50 & Progress bar translation and English layout: reorganized the terminal output progress tracking to a clean 3-line print format using standard English labels (`Integrating`, `step`, `steps/s`) to display runtime physics parameters and step counts in real time. \\
720: V51 & Legend layout alignment: vertically aligned the top edges of the time and external field HUD boxes; redesigned the field arrow to have a constant length and placed it inside the field box at the top right (adjacent to the label), ensuring visibility even at very small fields. \\
721: V52 & English translation: fully translated all remaining Portuguese console/terminal logs printed during initialization, physical parameters display, and simulation completion to English. \\
722: V53 & Circular direction dial and sign indicator: added a circular direction dial at the top right of the external field box and a sign indicator arrow next to the horizontal field intensity bar at the bottom right. \\
723: V54 & Developer metadata in terminal log: added code version and developer name to the simulation initialization banner. \\
724: V55 & HUD direction dial arrow scaling: scaled the arrow length within the circular dial proportionally to the normalized field intensity ($[-1, +1]$ relative to maximum field) and removed the bottom-right sign indicator arrow. \\
725: V56 & HUD direction dial arrow scaling minimum length calibration: defined a minimum arrow length ($0.35 R_{\mathrm{dial}}$) for active fields so that the shaft remains longer than the arrowhead at small fields, reaching full radius ($1.0 R_{\mathrm{dial}}$) at maximum field. \\

727: V58 & HUD direction dial bold arrow homothetic scaling: scaled the width, head width, and head length proportionally to the field intensity to preserve the arrow's aspect ratio (avoiding stubby rendering) as the field is reduced and inverted. \\
728: V59 & Random per-needle damping noise: added \code{--damping\_noise} parameter to introduce random variations in friction/damping for each individual needle, simulating realistic pivot differences. \\
729: V60 & Command-line interface translation: fully translated all remaining Portuguese help strings, warning messages, and parameter options in the program parser to English. \\
730: V61 & Section 4 plot string translation: translated all remaining Portuguese label, axis, and title strings in the hysteresis and sinusoidal plotting functions to English. \\

\paragraph{Simulator capabilities (current state, V67).}
The simulator supports three lattice geometries (square, triangular, honeycomb); \textbf{seven} external-field modes: static; First-Order Reversal Curve (FORC) mode with sat/reversal field parameter control; pulse with explicit timing (delay $\Delta t$ $\to$ field for $t_{\mathrm{pulse}}$ $\to$ zero field until equilibrium, with the legacy saturation/plateau criterion if $t_{\mathrm{pulse}}$ is not given); five-segment hysteresis ($0 \to +B \to 0 \to -B \to 0 \to +B$) with linear or log-symmetric spacing; sinusoidal field; and step modes \code{step\_pos} ($B{=}0$ for $\Delta t$, then field kept on) and \code{step\_neg} (field from $t{=}0$, removed at $\Delta t$).  \begin{abstract}

-This report documents the full development of the \code{compass\_sim} project: a Python simulator for two-dimensional arrays of magnetic compass needles interacting through complete dipolar coupling, with inertial Newtonian dynamics in SI units. The project began as a pedagogical demonstration of the analogy between compass arrays and magnetic materials, including hysteresis and domain formation, and evolved over six development sessions into a research instrument with publication potential. The report records the project decisions, problems encountered and solutions adopted, the code-version history (V20--V66), the research and publication strategy built around a gap identified in the literature, and the results of the pilot campaign on ``damping~$\times$~hysteresis/avalanches''. To help diagnose the issue, could you share the **exact command line** you executed? 

Here are the most likely causes and explanations for what you are experiencing:

### 1. Reaches 100% Instantaneously
For a $20 \times 20$ array (400 needles) running on a modern CPU, the optimized Verlet integration loop (using the precomputed V40 dipolar tensor) is extremely fast. For example, a simulation with $t_{\mathrm{sim}} = 4.0\text{ s}$ executes exactly 1,084 steps and takes only **0.17 seconds** to complete, which is why the progress bar appears to jump to 100% instantly.

### 2. Files Not Producing
When running `python3 compass.py` directly with `--field_mode forc`, it generates:
* **`forc_curve.csv`** (the raw data file containing `t_s`, `B_T`, `M_proj`, and `S`)
* **`hysteresis_loop.png`** (if `--make_images 1` is active)
* **`compass_field_log.csv`**

These files are saved directly in the **current working directory** from which you ran the terminal command.

### 3. Check for Common Pitfalls
* **Wrong Version Executable**: Make sure you are calling **`python3 compass.py`** or **`python3 compass_simV67.py`**. If you run `python3 compass_simV66.py` (which does not contain the FORC implementation), it will not run this mode.
* **Sweep Campaign Scripts**: The sweep orchestrator scripts (`damping_sweep.py` and `damping_sweepV02.py`) are dedicated specifically to Stage 1 (major hysteresis loop) and Stage 2 (relaxation/domains) and do not support the FORC protocol. FORC mode must be executed directly via `compass.py`.

Please share your command line so we can replicate and troubleshoot if you are still not seeing the generated files!

I have modified the implementation in [compass.py](file:///Users/jps/Dropbox/simula%20agulhas/compass.py) to simulate the **complete family (suite) of First-Order Reversal Curves (FORCs)** sequentially in a single simulation run, matching the exact protocol described in the literature.

### 1. Updated FORC Sweep Logic:
* **Automatic Time Overriding**: The total simulation time is automatically computed as:
  $$t_{\mathrm{sim}} = N_{\mathrm{curves}} \cdot (t_{\mathrm{sat}} + t_{\mathrm{ramp\_down}} + t_{\mathrm{ramp\_up}})$$
  This ensures you do not need to guess or calculate `--t_sim` manually when running the suite.
* **Regular Field Spacing**: The simulator automatically segments the timeline into $N_{\mathrm{curves}}$ cycles. In each cycle $k$, it saturates the array at $+B_{\max}$, ramps it down to a reversal field $B_{r, k}$ (evenly spaced from $+B_{\max}$ down to the minimum reversal field $B_{r,\mathrm{min}}$), and sweeps it back up to $+B_{\max}$.
* **Reversal Field Logging (`B_r`)**: The output files **`forc_curve.csv`** and **`compass_field_log.csv`** now record the active reversal field $B_{r, k}$ as a **fifth column** (`B_r`). This makes it simple to segment individual curves during post-processing.

### 2. New CLI Parameters in V67:
* **`--forc_n_curves`**: Number of reversal curves in the suite (Default: `30`).
* **`--forc_Br_min`**: Minimum reversal field $B_{r,\mathrm{min}}$ in Tesla (Default: $-B_{\max}$).
* **`--forc_t_sat`**: Saturation hold duration per cycle (Default: `0.05` s).
* **`--forc_t_ramp_down`**: Ramp-down duration from saturation to reversal field (Default: `0.10` s).
* **`--forc_t_ramp_up`**: Ramp-up sweep duration back to saturation (Default: `0.20` s).

### 3. Report Compilation and Code Freezing:
